diagrams.title: Operate the Domain Inventory-to-Cash Loop
diagrams.subtitle: Five controlled handoffs from sourcing to renewal or exit.
diagrams.assumptions_note: The core pod is one full-time owner plus one contractor. First-deal timing is 2–9 months; a completed sourcing cycle does not establish buyer demand or immediate liquidity.
diagrams.caption: Recognized operator revenue is gross domain sale proceeds. Escrow balances awaiting release and unsold asking prices are not completed-sale revenue.

stages.label: Source
stages.detail: Monitor NameBio comparables, expired-name lists, and drop-catch auctions; record extension, sale date, venue, buyer use case, and maximum bid.

stages.label: Screen
stages.detail: Use USPTO Trademark Search, ICANN Lookup, RDAP, and Wayback Machine records; reject mark-targeting theses and investigate conflicting historical use.

stages.label: Acquire
stages.value: Cap bids against total carrying exposure
stages.detail: Include auction fees, transfer charges, premium renewals, and expected holding periods in the bid ceiling; record registrar access and ownership evidence.

stages.label: Market
stages.value: Route inquiries into a priced negotiation
stages.detail: Publish consistent marketplace and landing-page prices; route inquiries to one owner and record buyer identity, offer history, and net settlement math.

stages.label: Settle and recycle
stages.value: Verify payment, transfer, and renewal decisions
stages.detail: Verify escrow instructions independently, follow registrar transfer procedures, reconcile released proceeds, and reassess unsold names before renewal.

diagrams.title: Track Domains Through One Nested Annual Cohort
diagrams.subtitle: Count unique domains, not messages, leads, or auction impressions.
diagrams.assumptions_note: Illustrative annual cohort: 400 researched domains, 100 screen-cleared domains, 40 owned and listed domains, 20 with qualified inquiries, and eight completed sales. Each stage is a subset of the preceding stage. Existing holdings may enter the researched cohort; listing is not necessarily a current-year acquisition.
diagrams.caption: Eight sales at an assumed $20,000 average produce the $160,000 Base-Case gross revenue. The implied 20% annual sell-through of 40 listed domains is a demanding modeling assumption, not a market benchmark.

stages.label: Researched domains
stages.detail: Deduplicate by domain and retain a dated record of comparable sales, intended use, carrying cost, and seller or auction provenance.

stages.label: Screen-cleared domains
stages.detail: Retain only domains passing documented rights, historical-use, pricing, and transferability checks; screen clearance does not authorize an unlimited bid.

stages.label: Owned and listed domains
stages.detail: Confirm control of every listed name, synchronize prices across venues, and remove stale listings immediately after a sale or ownership change.

stages.label: Domains with qualified inquiries
stages.detail: Count each domain once after a buyer demonstrates a credible use case and willingness to discuss price; exclude automated spam and duplicate contacts.

stages.label: Completed domain sales
stages.detail: Count only completed transactions; eight multiplied by $20,000 equals $160,000 gross proceeds, with acquisition and operating costs deducted separately.

diagrams.title: Reconcile $160,000 Gross Sales to $44,000 Owner Net
diagrams.subtitle: Six bars establish the Base-Case 27.5% annual net margin.
diagrams.assumptions_note: The canonical Base Case fixes gross revenue at $160,000 and annual owner net profit at $44,000. The four expense buckets below are an illustrative allocation of the required $116,000 total cost, not additional scorecard facts. Intermediate bars are signed deductions; the final bar is an absolute total.
diagrams.caption: $160,000 - $60,000 - $12,000 - $24,000 - $20,000 = $44,000; $44,000 / $160,000 = 27.5%. Conservative: $20,000 at 15% yields $3,000 with 1 FT + 1 C. Scaled: $300,000 at 40% yields $120,000 with 2 FT + 2 C.

stages.label: Gross domain sale proceeds
stages.detail: Start with completed domain sales before selling fees; do not substitute portfolio asking prices, third-party merchant volume, or escrow deposits.

stages.label: Sold-domain acquisition basis
stages.detail: Assign purchase prices and acquisition fees to the domains sold; unsold inventory purchases remain a separate cash-use and inventory schedule.

stages.label: Portfolio renewals
stages.detail: Include current-period renewal charges across retained and sold inventory; remove any amounts already included in acquisition basis.

stages.label: Selling and settlement costs
stages.detail: Assume a blended 15% of gross proceeds covering marketplace commissions and settlement charges; replace this model rate with actual venue invoices.

stages.label: Other operating expense
stages.detail: Budget contractor support, research tools, outreach, and administration at approximately $1,667 monthly; exclude renewals and transaction fees counted above.

stages.label: Annual owner net profit
stages.detail: This absolute endpoint equals 27.5% of gross revenue; do not add it as another movement or describe gross sales as the owner's earnings.

diagrams.title: Compare Direct Contribution Across Domain Sale Routes
diagrams.subtitle: Five independent $10,000 sale examples; bar values are percentages.
diagrams.assumptions_note: All examples are hypothetical completed sales, not observed market yields. Direct contribution equals sale proceeds less acquisition, renewal, selling, and stated deal-specific costs. Shared overhead, unsold inventory, and holding time are excluded, so these percentages are not annual net margins.
diagrams.caption: Compare routes only after equalizing sale price and cost definitions. These independent examples do not replace the canonical 15%, 27.5%, and 40% annual net margins.

stages.label: Brandable via marketplace
stages.detail: $10,000 proceeds less $3,000 acquisition, $1,500 selling costs, and $100 renewals leaves $5,400; invented-word appeal still requires mark screening.

stages.label: Exact-match via marketplace
stages.detail: $10,000 proceeds less $4,000 acquisition, $1,500 selling costs, and $100 renewals leaves $4,400; descriptive wording does not eliminate rights conflicts.

stages.label: Expired-authority via marketplace
stages.detail: $10,000 proceeds less $5,000 acquisition, $1,500 selling costs, $100 renewals, and $400 historical-use research leaves $3,000; rankings can disappear.

stages.label: Drop-catch resale via marketplace
stages.detail: $10,000 proceeds less $4,500 acquisition including auction fees, $1,500 selling costs, $100 renewals, and $200 diligence leaves $3,700.

stages.label: Outbound upgrade via direct escrow
stages.detail: $10,000 proceeds less $3,500 acquisition, $300 assumed settlement costs, $100 renewals, and $600 outreach leaves $5,500; verify actual escrow pricing.

diagrams.title: Resolve Four Pre-Flight Rights and Execution Checks
diagrams.subtitle: Each checkpoint defines a proceed path and a stop-or-rework path.
diagrams.assumptions_note: Apply rights checks before bidding and repeat relevant checks before marketing and transfer. UDRP is a contractual domain dispute policy, distinct from statutory ACPA claims; registration availability does not establish lawful use.
diagrams.caption: Preserve dated evidence for acquisition intent, prior use, ownership, and outreach. Automated screening flags cases for review; it cannot establish the absence of disputes.

stages.label: Trademark and ACPA exposure
stages.value: Document clean rationale or reject acquisition
stages.detail: Review 15 U.S.C. 1114 and 1125, including 1125(d). Proceed with documented independent use rationale; reject a thesis built on bad-faith profit from another party's protected mark.

stages.label: Applicable domain dispute policy
stages.value: Check legitimate interests and adverse evidence
stages.detail: For UDRP-covered names, examine confusing similarity, rights or legitimate interests, and bad-faith registration and use under paragraph 4(a). Proceed after review; hold unresolved adverse facts.

stages.label: Control, transfer, and historical claims
stages.value: Verify deliverability or suspend the listing
stages.detail: Check registrar control, applicable transfer locks, expiration, and dispute status. Under 15 U.S.C. 45, substantiate traffic and authority claims; proceed with evidence or remove unsupported claims.

stages.label: Commercial-email execution
stages.value: Send compliant outreach or repair the campaign
stages.detail: Apply 15 U.S.C. 7704: accurate headers, nondeceptive subjects, required advertising identification, valid postal address, and working opt-out. Honor opt-outs within ten business days; suppress recipients before further campaigns.

diagrams.title: Keep the Core Pod Small and Add Two Seats Deliberately
diagrams.subtitle: Two core people; four people only in the scaled scenario.
diagrams.assumptions_note: Conservative and Base use one full-time owner plus one contractor. Scaled uses two full-time people plus two contractors. Each stage represents one person; the last two seats are additions, not hidden Base-Case staffing.
diagrams.caption: The owner retains bid limits, pricing authority, registrar control, and payout verification. Contractors receive only the access required for their assigned work.

stages.label: Core owner
stages.detail: Set portfolio budgets and bid ceilings, review rights risks, negotiate sales, control registrar credentials, and reconcile escrow releases.

stages.label: Core research contractor
stages.detail: Maintain comparable-sale records and renewal calendars; use spreadsheets or SQLite for inventory tracking without authority to transfer domains.

stages.label: Scaled sales operator
stages.detail: Handle inbound inquiry routing, qualification, documented offers, and lawful outbound upgrades within the owner's written pricing limits.

stages.label: Scaled operations contractor
stages.value: Add 1 C; monitoring and reconciliation support
stages.detail: Automate renewal reminders and comparable-sale monitoring; audit listing consistency and transaction records without unilateral payout or transfer access.

diagrams.title: Allocate a $30,000 Reference Startup Budget Across Four Buckets
diagrams.subtitle: Compare $8,000 lean, $30,000 reference, and $60,000 expanded plans.
diagrams.assumptions_note: This illustrative $30,000 reference opening cash allocation sits within the $8,000–$60,000 USD startup capital range; it is not a required portfolio size or an annual expense forecast. Numeric values are reference-plan dollars. Each plan allocates 50% to acquisition inventory, 10% to research and transaction setup, 10% to renewal and transfer reserves, and 30% to operating runway. Lean and expanded amounts are shown in each bucket. Do not add these buckets to the annual waterfall as though all cash deployed were current expense.
diagrams.caption: Lean: $4,000 + $800 + $800 + $2,400 = $8,000. Reference: $15,000 + $3,000 + $3,000 + $9,000 = $30,000. Expanded: $30,000 + $6,000 + $6,000 + $18,000 = $60,000. At $500–$5,000 monthly operating expense, the reference $9,000 operating reserve covers 1.8–18 months, excluding inventory purchases and separately reserved renewals and transfers.

stages.label: Acquisition inventory
stages.detail: Allocate $4,000 of the $8,000 lean plan, $15,000 of the $30,000 reference plan, or $30,000 of the $60,000 expanded plan. Deploy gradually into researched names and capped auction bids; retain a per-domain basis ledger rather than marking unsold inventory to asking prices.

stages.label: Research and transaction setup
stages.detail: Allocate $800 of the $8,000 lean plan, $3,000 of the $30,000 reference plan, or $6,000 of the $60,000 expanded plan. Reserve for comparable-sale tools, historical-use research, targeted rights review, and initial transaction setup; release funds against scoped work.

stages.label: Renewal and transfer reserve
stages.detail: Allocate $800 of the $8,000 lean plan, $3,000 of the $30,000 reference plan, or $6,000 of the $60,000 expanded plan. Ring-fence cash against registrar renewal schedules, premium-name charges, and transfer costs; revise the reserve as holdings and renewal dates change.

stages.label: Operating runway reserve
stages.detail: Allocate $2,400 of the $8,000 lean plan, $9,000 of the $30,000 reference plan, or $18,000 of the $60,000 expanded plan. Support contractor work, inquiry handling, and routine administration while sales remain uneven. First-deal timing is 2–9 months; the reference reserve covers nine months only at monthly operating expense of $1,000 or less. At $5,000 monthly, even the expanded operating reserve covers only 3.6 months.

diagrams.title: Build an Auditable Domain Desk in Thirty Days
diagrams.subtitle: Four weekly milestones establish operations, not a promised sale.
diagrams.assumptions_note: The launch sprint creates evidence, controls, and listings. Canonical first-deal timing remains 2–9 months. Buying inventory during the sprint is conditional on completed diligence and available carrying reserves.
diagrams.caption: Exit day 30 with documented buy rules, controlled inventory, working inquiry routing, and a renewal calendar; report actual offers and settlements separately from asking prices.

stages.label: Days 1-7
stages.value: Define the thesis and capital limits
stages.detail: Choose one primary niche, document buyer use cases, build a comparable-sales worksheet, allocate startup cash, and set per-name and portfolio bid ceilings.

stages.label: Days 8-14
stages.value: Complete diligence and secure operating accounts
stages.detail: Record trademark and historical-use checks, review auction terms, enable registrar multifactor authentication, and create dated acquisition decisions before placing authorized bids.

stages.label: Days 15-21
stages.value: Publish controlled inventory and route inquiries
stages.detail: List only owned names, synchronize venue prices, test contact routing, maintain opt-out suppression, and verify escrow and transfer procedures without initiating a test ownership transfer.

stages.label: Days 22-30
stages.value: Audit unit economics and the renewal runway
stages.detail: Reconcile actual spending, inspect qualified inquiries, calculate transaction-level contribution, schedule 90-, 60-, and 30-day renewal reminders, and define next-month retain-or-drop decisions.
